I see that we can define the inverse of a function with docs#Function.invFun .

I also see that the normal notation for inverses, ⁻¹, doesn't work. (Failed to synthesize instance of typeclass Inv (α → β).) I remember that the namespace Function.<whatever> behaved weirdly because, as I recall, "Function" isn't the same kind of type that gets used in other namespaces that hope to allow for generalized field notation. Many different kinds of things are modeled as functions.

Is this flexibility in what counts as a Function related to the lack of inverse notation for things that I want to think of as functions? Or is this more of a case where, if I had some other facts milling around in the type system, the notation f⁻¹ would start working?

docs#Inv.inv goes from a type to itself, but f.invFun does not have the same type as f in general. There is the inv notation for docs#Equiv.Perm though, and docs#Equiv.symm is the inverse operation for the type of bijections.

It's worth pointing out that docs#Function.invFun generally isn't what you want. If you have a bijection between types it's often more convenient to use docs#Equiv, which indeed gives you docs#Equiv.symm for the inverse function.
